# Exact lean-number spectrum of cyclic three-configurations generated by \(\{0,1,3\}\)

## Finding

**Theorem.** For every integer \(n\ge7\), let \(H_n\) be the labelled, simple, \(3\)-uniform hypergraph with vertex set \(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\) and the \(n\) edges
\[
 e_i=\{i,i+1,i+3\}\pmod n,\qquad i\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z.
\]
A *lean coloring* assigns at least two colors to the vertices, and on each edge the three colors are either identical or pairwise different. The lean number \(\lambda(H_n)\) is the least number of colors in such a coloring. Then
\[
\boxed{\lambda(H_n)=\begin{cases}5,&n=7,\\3,&n\ge8\text{ and }8\mid n,\\4,&n\ge8\text{ and }8\nmid n.\end{cases}}
\]
When \(8\mid n\), there are **exactly \(24\)** named optimal lean colorings with a fixed three-color palette. They are precisely the nonconstant solutions of \(c_i+c_{i+1}+c_{i+3}=0\) over \(\mathbb F_3\); every one is eight-periodic and has exactly \(n/4\) monochromatic edges. In particular, none is a strong three-coloring. For \(n=7\) there are exactly \(840\) named optimal lean colorings with a fixed five-color palette. For every \(n\ge8\) an explicit four-color lean coloring exists.

## Assumptions and scope

The hypergraph is labelled and no edges are repeated. For \(n\ge7\), the three entries in every edge are distinct and the \(n\) translates are pairwise distinct. "Uses \(q\) colors" means that exactly \(q\) distinct colors appear, although enumerations with a fixed \(q\)-symbol palette would give the same result at the minimum. A named coloring distinguishes color labels. The two-section graph of \(H_n\) has edges between vertices appearing together in a triple; it equals the third power of the cycle \(C_n^3\). The results make no claims about other cyclic generators or nonlinear coloring rules.

## Proof

**1. Two colors are impossible.** If only two colors are available, a permitted triple cannot have three different colors, so each edge must be monochromatic. Since the edges link consecutive vertices, the hypergraph is connected, hence every vertex has the same color. Thus no lean coloring uses two colors.

**2. Three-color linearization.** Label three available colors by \(\mathbb F_3\). For three field elements \(a,b,c\), the condition that they are all equal or all distinct is equivalent to \(a+b+c=0\) in \(\mathbb F_3\): both allowed patterns sum to zero; a two-equal-one-different pattern has nonzero sum. Thus an assignment on \(H_n\) is permissible exactly when
\[
 c_i+c_{i+1}+c_{i+3}=0\quad\text{for all }i\pmod n.
\]
Let \(T\) denote cyclic shift of coordinates and \(p(t)=1+t+t^3\). The ternary solution space is \(\ker p(T)\). The standard cyclic-module identification \(\mathbb F_3^n\cong\mathbb F_3[t]/(t^n-1)\) gives
\[
 \dim\ker p(T)=\deg\gcd(p(t),t^n-1).
\]
Indeed, writing \(d=\gcd(p,t^n-1)\), annihilation modulo \(t^n-1\) means divisibility by \((t^n-1)/d\), leaving exactly \(\deg d\) free coefficients. This holds even if \(3\mid n\), when \(t^n-1\) may have repeated roots.

**3. Exact arithmetic threshold.** Over \(\mathbb F_3\),
\[
 p(t)=(t-1)(t^2+t+2).
\]
The quadratic is irreducible. If \(\alpha\) is either root, direct reduction gives \(\alpha^4=2=-1\), so \(\alpha\) has multiplicative order eight. Since \(p\) is square-free, its common factors with \(t^n-1\) have degrees one when \(8\nmid n\), and three when \(8\mid n\). The number of solutions is therefore \(3\) or \(27\). In either case three solutions are constant. Every nonconstant solution uses all three colors by Step 1; therefore there are no lean three-colorings unless \(8\mid n\), and then there are exactly \(27-3=24\).

Moreover, \(p(t)\) divides \(t^8-1\), so \((T^8-I)c=0\) for any solution: it is eight-periodic. Every eight-periodic solution with all three colors is obtained by assigning its first three colors and iterating \(c_{i+3}=-c_i-c_{i+1}\). Up to affine permutations \(z\mapsto uz+v\) of \(\mathbb F_3\), with \(u\in\{1,2\}\) and \(v\in\mathbb F_3\), its period-eight word is one of

| Representative period-eight word | Monochromatic edge indices modulo eight |
| --- | --- |
| `00102212` | \(0,4\) |
| `01022120` | \(3,7\) |
| `01121002` | \(1,5\) |
| `01220211` | \(2,6\) |

Each word obeys the recurrence, and the four affine orbits have six words each, exhausting the 24 possibilities. Thus each period contains exactly two monochromatic edges, giving \(n/4\) among \(n\) edges.

**4. Explicit four-color upper bound for every \(n\ge8\).** Use the four distinct colors \(0,1,2,3\). The four cyclic words

| Length | Cyclic word |
| --- | --- |
| \(4\) | `0123` |
| \(9\) | `012202311` |
| \(10\) | `0122321003` |
| \(11\) | `01220213323` |

all satisfy the lean triple condition with indices taken cyclically within their respective lengths, and all begin with `012`. To verify arbitrary concatenations of these words, the only new triples to examine at a boundary are those starting at the last three indices of the preceding block; if its final three symbols are \((a,b,c)\), these three triples are \((a,b,0)\), \((b,c,1)\), and \((c,0,2)\). The possible final triples are respectively `123`, `311`, `003`, and `323`; direct substitution shows every boundary triple is either monochromatic or rainbow. This also handles the closing boundary of the cyclic concatenation.

For \(n\ge8\) divisible by four, concatenate \(n/4\) copies of the length-four word. For other residues modulo four, start with the word of length \(9\), \(10\), or \(11\), respectively, and append enough length-four words to reach \(n\). The resulting cyclic word is lean and uses at most four colors. If \(8\nmid n\), Step 3 makes three colors impossible, so the construction uses exactly four colors and is optimal.

**5. Seven vertices.** When \(n=7\), the seven edges comprise the Fano Steiner triple system: all six nonzero differences of \(\{0,1,3\}\) modulo seven are distinct, so every pair of vertices occurs in exactly one edge. In any lean coloring, a color class containing two vertices also contains the unique third vertex on their line, since a triple with two equal colors cannot be rainbow. If such a class contained a fourth vertex, closure under all Fano lines would force the entire seven-point set to have that color: two intersecting lines in the class already generate the Fano plane. Thus every nontrivial color class has size either one or three, and at most one three-point color class can occur, because any two Fano lines meet. A nonconstant coloring therefore needs at least five colors. Taking one Fano line monochromatic and assigning distinct new colors to its four complementary vertices attains five. There are exactly seven choices of line, five choices of its color and \(4!\) assignments of the other colors, yielding \(7\cdot5\cdot4!=840\) named optimal colorings. This proves all cases.

**6. Comparison with strong coloring.** Because every triple has all pairwise differences \(1,2,3\), the two-section is \(C_n^3\). For \(8\mid n\), four consecutive cycle vertices form a clique, while the periodic four-coloring \(i\mapsto i\bmod4\) is proper, so \(\chi(C_n^3)=4\). The lean number is three for these same lengths, and every optimal lean coloring has \(n/4\) monochromatic triples. Thus the strict three-versus-four gap is genuine and persists along all multiples of eight; the broader strong-color spectrum of this same family was previously determined by Erskine (2021), so the strong-color classification itself is not claimed as new.

## Verification

The accompanying standalone `verify.py` enumerates ternary incidence kernels independently by Gaussian elimination, compares their dimensions with polynomial greatest common divisors for 560 small cyclic systems, exhaustively compares 56 systems with direct three-color search, checks all lean colorings of the seven-point system using three, four, and five colors, and verifies representative solution counts and monochromatic-edge counts. The same program checks the four-color constructions for every \(8\le n\le300\), yielding `VERIFY_OK`. These finite computations reproduce the claims in their checked ranges; the algebraic and concatenation proofs above establish the infinite assertions.

## Relationship to prior work

Piehowski (2026) introduces the lean number and studies general uniform hypergraphs, including connected cases and overlap constructions. The present explicit all-order cyclic-configuration spectrum and named optimum counts were not identified in the inspected primary discussion. The cyclic generator \(\{0,1,3\}\) is classical: Bašić, Grošelj, Grünbaum and Pisanski (2018) identify its Levi graphs at orders seven and eight with the Fano/Heawood and Möbius–Kantor instances, respectively, while investigating configuration splittability rather than lean coloring. Erskine (2021, Theorems 2.5 and 3.4) directly studies the **same** cyclic configurations and determines blocking-set parameters and the complete **strong** chromatic-number spectrum, equal to seven at order seven, six at order eleven, four at multiples of four, and five at other orders. This does not determine their different lean-number spectrum: strong colorings require every triple rainbow, whereas lean colorings permit monochromatic triples but forbid the two-equal-one-distinct pattern. The strong-color classification therefore gives an upper bound but does not imply the stated sharper values, 24/840 optimum counts or the four-color constructions outside multiples of four. The equivalence of the monochromatic-or-rainbow ternary condition with a linear equation is also familiar in Fox tricoloring; that elementary equivalence is **not** claimed as new. The contribution assessed here is the complete lean-number classification for this infinite cyclic family, the eight-divisibility phase transition, and the exact optimal-coloring multiplicities. An equivalent result under other terminology cannot be excluded without further historical examination.

## Limitations

This result is confined to the specified cyclic three-configurations with \(n\ge7\). The values for general cyclic difference families, more than three uniform vertices, other lean-coloring invariants, and all optimal four-color enumeration are not established. The self-review is not an independent mathematical audit. Completeness of historical priority searches is not certified; in particular other treatments of ternary kernel colorings of cyclic configurations might overlap.
